xref.title: BBC Radiophonic Workshop Tenure (1962-1973)
xref.body: Delia Derbyshire joined the BBC Radiophonic Workshop in 1962, a facility that Daphne Oram had helped establish. She remained there for 11 years, during which she worked on electronic music for nearly 200 radio and television programs, becoming a pivotal figure in the history of electronic music. xref.title: "Doctor Who" Theme Arrangement (1963-1980)
xref.body: Delia Derbyshire's most famous work is her electronic arrangement of the "Doctor Who" theme. While composer Ron Granger wrote the original tune, Derbyshire was responsible for giving it its familiar and iconic electronic sound, which viewers heard from 1963 through 1980. Her reinterpretation is considered one of the most famous pieces of sci-fi music in the universe. "Her most famous work involved taking the theme from the BBC show Dr. Who and turning it into something entirely electronic."

xref.title: A Clockwork Orange (1972) Score
xref.body: Wendy Carlos, a classical musician who had been collaborating with Bob Moog on the development and application of his new modular synthesizers, was hired by director Stanley Kubrick to compose the score for his 1971 futuristic dystopian film, *A Clockwork Orange*. The entirely electronic score, released as a soundtrack in 1972 (with Carlos identifying as Walter Carlos at the time), introduced sounds no one had heard before and became a landmark in the widespread development of electronic music, influencing many rock musicians seeking novel sounds. "No one had ever heard such sounds. It was completely electronic."

xref.body: New Order showcased considerable influence from David Bowie, particularly in their electronic and New Wave soundscapes. "You could see lots of Bowie influence in Depeche Mode and the cure and new order."

xref.body: Brian Eno produced all three of David Bowie's Berlin records, a collaboration that further cemented Eno's reputation as one of the most innovative and important producers in the world. xref.title: Broad Cultural Influence
xref.body: Bowie's influence extends beyond music, impacting style, image, concert performance, fashion, film, stage, painting, museums, and even career management. His work significantly affected various music genres like rock, punk, new wave, goth, industrial, electronic music, dance, grunge, and indie rock. He is considered one of the most important figures for gay people in pop culture, with tremendous social and political implications, especially in the UK. "Bowie's influence can be found all over rock and punk and new wave, and goth, and industrial, and electronic music, dance, grunge, indie rock."

xref.title: Challenges of Early Live Performances (1970s-1980s)
xref.body: Performing live with early, finicky electronic gear was terrifying for the band, as something would invariably break down. Andy McCluskey resorted to telling jokes to the audience to fill the gaps while the band members frantically tried to fix or reprogram equipment. Monophonic synths required constant, difficult patching between songs using flashlights. "It was terrifying. Actually, it was terrifying and something would always break down. And I ended up having to have a collection of jokes to tell. The audience to fill in the gaps while they were trying to fix something or get something sorted out."

xref.title: Collaboration with Bob Moog
xref.body: Carlos worked closely with Bob Moog at the Columbia-Princeton Electronic Music Center, where she offered a crucial musician's perspective on the design and feel of his new electronic instruments. Her input was instrumental in decisions like incorporating a keyboard and refining the tactile experience of individual keys, making synthesizers more user-friendly for musicians. "She worked carefully with Bob Mogue, offering a musician's perspective, and how his new electronic instruments should look and feel."

xref.title: Commercial Peak of Technopop
xref.body: The Human League achieved a massive global hit in the winter of 1981-82, a period recognized as the commercial peak for Technopop music. Their success exemplified the genre's accessibility and danceability, bringing electronic sounds to a wide international audience. "There's the human leg with a massive global hit from the winter of 1981-82, which is the period when Technopop really reached its commercial peak."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Continuing Late 90s Electronica Trend
xref.body: The Chemical Brothers continued to be a presence in the 2000s, signifying the ongoing influence of late 90s electronica trends that fostered the re-emergence of dance and electronic elements within alt rock. "The prodigy and the chemical brothers were still with us, so as Fatboy Slim."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Cultural Impact - Redefining Rock Stardom
xref.body: David Bowie profoundly changed culture by subverting the traditional meaning of a rock star, pushing music into new realms of theater and spectacle. His continuously shape-shifting style was widely imitated by artists like Madonna and Lady Gaga, and he served as a crucial inspiration for punk, new wave, post-punk, electronic, goth, industrial, and alternative movements, including bands like the Pixies, Nirvana, Nine Inch Nails, and Arcade Fire. "David Bowie irrevocably changed our culture. He began by subverting what it meant to be a rock star."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Curator of 1980s Soundtracks (1980s)
xref.body: John Hughes was known for creating soundtracks for his "brat pack" movies that featured alternative music, often British and electronic. He believed these sounds suited the "outsider" characters in his films, leading him to collaborate with bands like OMD, New Order, Simple Minds, and Kim Wilde. "I suspect that the soundtracks that he put together, which were very often British and quite often electronic, would be the sort of alternative music that those kids in the films would listen to."

xref.body: As the drummer for New Order, Stephen Morris undertook the task of learning how to program the new generation of drum machines. xref.body: Echo & the Bunnymen utilized a drum machine in their performances, rather than a flesh-and-blood drummer. xref.title: Drum Machine in Encores
xref.body: Stephen Morris's drum machine was utilized by New Order to play automatically during encores, allowing the band members to depart the stage earlier. "just turning on Stephen Morris' drum machine and letting it go while everybody walked off stage"

xref.title: Early German Electronic Musicians
xref.body: Tangerine Dream was among the German groups that began creating electronic music in the early 1970s, seeking to establish a unique musical identity separate from the prevailing British and American rock and roll. This development was significantly aided by the experimental electronic studio built by West German Radio, which had exposed German musicians to electronic sounds for nearly two decades. "There were groups like Cannes and Tangerine Dream, and most important of all, Kraftwerk."

xref.body: Butch Vig grew up in Verlacua, Wisconsin. He took piano lessons as a child and later picked up the drums as a teenager. His academic path included two years in pre-med at the University of Wisconsin, followed by four semesters of electronic music theory, before he decided to drop out and pursue music. xref.title: Electronic Music Pioneer at BBC Radiofonc Workshop
xref.body: Delia Derbyshire worked at the BBC Radiofonc Workshop for 11 years, starting in 1962. During her tenure, she composed electronic music for nearly 200 radio and TV programs, utilizing tape machines, oscillators, and sine wave generators in her experimental compositions until 1975, making significant contributions to the field. "She stayed there for 11 years, working on electronic music for close to 200 radio and TV programs, using tape machines and oscillators and sine wave generators, whatever she could get her hands on."

xref.title: Electronic Music Pioneers and Influences
xref.body: Kraftwerk was incredibly important and influential in the development of electronic music, with many genres and ideas flowing from their work, including Technopop, Industrial Music, and elements of Hip Hop. They were instrumental in establishing the idea that electronics were as viable as guitars for making rock and roll, and their clean, thematic approach to albums made them worthy of deep study. "Kraftwerk was incredibly important and incredibly influential when it came to the whole idea of electronic music."

xref.body: Guitars and real drums have periodically fallen in and out of favor with Depeche Mode; there was a significant period in their career where their sound was 100% electronic and synthesized. In their very early days in the late 1970s, guitars were part of their sound but were seen as restrictive and logistically difficult to transport compared to synthesizers. "One we felt that guitars restricted us. The sound of the guitars very limited. And we found synthesizers very interesting, just the sounds that you could get on them."

xref.body: Initially resembling Joy Division with dark, guitar-driven music, New Order quickly embraced synth pop sounds, drawing inspiration from Kraftwerk and other German bands. Over time, they incorporated more electronics, drum machines, synthesizers, and samplers, moving towards a more electronic sound. "But they very soon started bringing in synth pop sounds that owed more to a nod to craftwork and a few other German bands."

xref.body: Sonic Youth was cited as an example of "low-fi, fuzzy guitar rock," illustrating the broad stylistic range encompassed by the "alternative" umbrella. xref.title: Exemplar of 1980s Drum Sound
xref.body: The band, featuring Robert Palmer, members of Duran Duran, and drummer Tony Thompson, is highlighted as a prime example of the pervasive drum sound of the 1980s. This sound was characterized by its big, boomy, and powerful quality, often achieved by recording in large, reverberant rooms and augmenting with electronic effects like gated reverbs. "The Power Station featuring Robert Palmer, a couple of guys from Durandoran and drummer Tony Thompson. That is an example of the drum sound that was very much invoked in the 1980s."

xref.body: Stockhausen is recognized as a highly influential German composer and one of the most important experimental musicians of the 20th century, especially for his pioneering work in electronic music. xref.title: First All-Electronic Score
xref.body: In 1957, Daphne Oram created the soundtrack for her play titled "Ampatrium 38," marking it as the first-ever all-electronic score for any production. This achievement highlighted her innovative approach to musical composition and laid a foundation for electronic sound in media. "In 1957, she created the soundtrack for her play entitled Ampatrium 38, which was the first ever all electronic score for anything."

xref.body: In 1957, Daphne Oram composed the soundtrack for the play *Amphitrium 38*, which is recognized as the first-ever entirely electronic score for any production. xref.body: Plus 44 was formed by Mark Hoppus and Travis Barker during Blink-182's hiatus, initially conceived as a more electronic project. The band's name, "Plus 44," was inspired by the international dialing code for the United Kingdom, where the idea for the band first germinated among its members. xref.body: In a true demonstration of the "do-it-yourself" ethos, Black Flag decided to form their own record label, SST Records, when no major label would sign them. xref.body: Daphne Oram was instrumental in convincing the BBC to establish an electronic workshop, which became known as the BBC Radiophonic Workshop, where further experimentation in electronic music ensued. xref.body: Afrika Bambaataa is widely recognized as one of the founding fathers of rap, particularly for his influential track "Planet Rock." This song's innovative use of electronic sounds and sampling, including a Kraftwerk sample, profoundly shaped the direction of hip hop and related genres. "And he is recognized as one of the founding fathers of rap."

xref.body: Kraftwerk is recognized for their foundational influence on rap music, particularly through Afrika Bambaataa's sampling of their work in "Planet Rock." Their pioneering electronic sounds provided a template for future hip hop and dance genres. "And by extension, we must give respect to craft work."

xref.title: Founding Her Own Studio for New Sounds
xref.body: After leaving the BBC in 1959, Daphne Oram established her own studio devoted to creating new electronic sounds. Her work there extended to film, where she produced all the electronic sound effects for the first three James Bond movies: "Dr. No," "From Russia with Love," and "Goldfinger," showcasing her unique sonic artistry. "When she left the Beebe in 1959, she founded her own studio devoted to creating new sounds."

xref.title: From Organization to Power Plant
xref.body: Kraftwerk emerged from the ashes of the experimental group Organization. Its name, "Kraftwerk," is German for "power plant." Founding members Ralf Hütter and Florian Schneider, originally classical music students, developed a keen interest in synthesizers and began experimenting with synth and drum machine music, leading to their unique all-electronic sound. "Organization, remember that band we talked about? It became Kraftwerk, which is German for power plant."

xref.title: Gateway via Moroder
xref.body: For those who became interested in electronic music through the work of Giorgio Moroder, it was a relatively short step to discover and appreciate Kraftwerk. xref.title: Iconic "Doctor Who" Theme Arrangement
xref.body: Her most famous work is the electronic arrangement of the theme song for the BBC show "Dr. Who." Although the music was written by composer Ron Grainer, Delia Derbyshire transformed it into its familiar electronic sound, which was heard by viewers at the start of every episode from 1963 to 1980, making it one of the most famous TV theme songs ever. "But she is the one who gave it that familiar electronic arrangement."

xref.title: Immense Influence on New Rock
xref.body: David Bowie is considered uniquely influential in the world of New Rock, with his work in the 1970s being traceable as a root for genres like punk, new wave, industrial, and electronic music. His influence is evident in the sound and vision of numerous bands including Nirvana, the Sex Pistols, Foo Fighters, Nine Inch Nails, R.E.M., Smashing Pumpkins, The Killers, Scott Weiland, and Coldplay. xref.title: Influence of German Identity
xref.body: Growing up in post-World War II Germany, with a complex and "confused sense of identity" exacerbated by the denazification period, young musicians like Kraftwerk aimed to forge a new musical identity. Their goal was to create music not beholden to American or UK influences, leading them to embrace the modern electronic music of their homeland, often abandoning traditional rock instrumentation. "Their goal came to be the creation of a new form of music that wasn't beholden to what was happening in America or the UK."

xref.title: Influence on David Bowie

xref.title: Influence on David Bowie's Berlin Period

xref.title: Influential Robotic Sound
xref.body: Kraftwerk's music from the late 1970s, exemplified by "The Model," was characterized by a robotic, cold, deliberately artificial, emotionally sterile, and intense vibe. This sound was a significant part of early Technopop and greatly intrigued and influenced artists like David Bowie. "And note the vibe of that song. Much of early technopop was robotic, cold, deliberately artificial, emotionally sterile, and just generally a little intense. That description can also be applied to craft work, the normal and some of Bowie's electronic experiments."

xref.title: Intentional Sonic Reinvention (Kid A)
xref.body: For "Kid A," Radiohead intentionally "burned it all down and they started from scratch," fundamentally changing their sound to an electronic record. This involved minimal guitar use by Ed O'Brien and Jonny Greenwood, Phil Selway acting more as a computer programmer, and Tom Yorke creating vocals via self-written computer programs. They successfully "destroyed themselves and rebuilt the band as something brand new." "they burned it all down and they started from scratch, which is not an easy thing to do."

"These guys, a British jazz dude working for the BBC and an American record producer, were huge influences on the world of electronic music, but they were almost entirely behind the scenes."

xref.title: Investment in Ampex and Tape Recording
xref.body: Bing Crosby became an investor in Ampex, an electronic firm that manufactured reel-to-reel machines based on Jack Mullin's German technology. Crosby was motivated by his dislike for having to repeat his national radio show for the West Coast time zone and saw tape recording as a solution to pre-tape his East Coast broadcast. His investment was crucial in developing modern studio techniques. "So Bing became an investor in Ampex, an electronic firm that had been making real-to-real machines based on Moin's German booty."

xref.title: Lack of Royalties for Amen Break
xref.body: Despite the Amen Break from "Amen Brother" being sampled in over 5,309 songs and becoming a major part of numerous hits across hip-hop, electronic, and EDM, neither Gregory Coleman nor The Winston's received any royalties. Gregory Coleman died homeless and broke in 2006, unaware of his profound impact on music, and band leader Richard Spencer died in 2020. "Not as the case with so many samples, neither Coleman nor the Winston's have seen any royalties from this, despite the fact that this piece of music has become part of so many other songs, some of which, many of which have become major hits."

xref.title: Move to Berlin - Cold War Artistic Hub
xref.body: In an effort to escape the negative influences surrounding him in L.A. and kick his cocaine addiction, Bowie and Iggy Pop moved to Berlin, Germany. During the height of the Cold War, Berlin was a divided city, yet its unique artistic and bohemian culture provided the perfect environment for Bowie's musical evolution, where he immersed himself in German electronic and crude rock sounds. "He and Iggy Pop packed up and left for Berlin. Now Berlin. Nobody went to Berlin. This was the height of the Cold War."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Move to West Berlin with Iggy Pop
xref.body: Deeply influenced by German electronic groups like Kraftwerk, Can, and Neu!, and envisioning electronic music as the future, Bowie moved to West Berlin with Iggy Pop to immerse themselves in the local scene and simultaneously recover from their addictions. They settled in a modest place at Hopstresser 155 in the Schöneberg area, motivated by a belief that remaining in Los Angeles would lead to their demise. "He began to think that these electronic methods of producing music were the future. And what better way to follow this muse than to move to where it all seemed to be happening? Germany."

xref.body: After World War II, Oram deeply explored composing with synthetic sounds, utilizing esoteric audio equipment like sine wave oscillators combined with magnetic tape recorders, as synthesizers had not yet been invented. Her studio was described as resembling something from a science fiction movie. "So she used things like sine wave oscillators combined with magnetic tape recorders. Her studio must have looked like something out of a science fiction movie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pioneering Electronic Music with TONTO
xref.body: In the late 1960s, Malcolm Cecil, a British jazz musician working for the BBC, along with American record producer Robert Margouleff, were fascinated by new synthesizers from Bob Moog. They set out to construct the world's largest modular synth setup, which they named TONTO (The Original New Timbral Orchestra). This behemoth, comprising gear from Moog, Oberheim, ARP, EMS, Roland, and Yamaha, allowed for unprecedented sound creation and multi-track performance, profoundly influencing electronic music. "These guys, a British jazz dude working for the BBC and an American record producer, were huge influences on the world of electronic music, but they were almost entirely behind the scenes."

They embarked on creating TONTO (The Original New Timbral Orchestra), the world's largest modular synth setup. This colossal instrument, built with components from various manufacturers, enabled unprecedented sonic textures and multi-layered compositions, significantly impacting electronic music production. xref.title: Pioneering Electronic Sound
xref.body: Starting in the early 1970s, Kraftwerk, an all-electronic band from Dusseldorf, West Germany, developed cold, robotic, minimalist, futuristic, and sometimes pessimistic and dystopian sounds. Their work laid the foundational groundwork for a vast range of future music genres including technopop, industrial music, hip hop, and even disco. "Starting in the early 70s, they said about creating some cold, robotic, minimalist, futuristic, and sometimes pessimistic and dystopian sounds that would end up laying the foundations for everything from technopop to industrial music to hip hop to, yeah, even disco in the years ahead."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pioneering Electronic Sounds
xref.body: Kraftwerk pioneered the use of synthesizers to create entirely artificial sounds like square waves, which differed significantly from traditional "nice, smooth, rounded waveforms." These explorations led to the generation of unique and "very cool" sonic textures. "Instead of nice, smooth, rounded waveforms, these things could generate square waves, totally artificial sounds and very cool ones."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pioneering German Electronic Music
xref.body: In the 1960s, West German artists like Kraftwerk sought to develop a unique musical style that diverged from American and British sounds, leading many to embrace electronic sounds. Kraftwerk emerged as the most influential among them, achieving best-selling albums and international chart success that significantly drew attention to electronic music. "But special props must go to craft work. In the 1960s, Germans, or more correctly West Germans, we're looking for a style of music that they could call their own."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pioneering Synthesizer Use
xref.body: Kraftwerk demonstrated how synthesizers could be utilized for purposes beyond experimental music or sound effects for planetarium shows, influencing subsequent electronic music artists. "Meanwhile, groups such as Kraftworth were demonstrating how synthesizer sounds could be used for something other than experimental music and sound effects for planetarium shows."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pioneers of Industrial Music
xref.body: Cabaret Voltaire helped create Industrial Music, a heavy form of electronic music, contributing to the diverse output of Factory Records. "Cabaret Voltaire, who helped create the heavy form of electronic music called Industrial Music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pioneers of New Romanticism
xref.body: Spandau Ballet emerged from the vibrant British club scene of Billies and The Blitz Club, which served as breeding grounds for groups associated with the New Romantic movement. This offshoot of synth-based music was characterized by its distinctive style and electronic sound. "One such offshoot was known as New Romantic, which had its roots in a couple of British clubs dedicated to new music. One was called Billies, and the other was the Blitz Club. This was the breeding site of groups like Spandovalet, Visage, and Culture Club."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Post-Peak Technopop Persistence
xref.body: As the popularity of pure Technopop waned in the mid-1980s, Bronski Beat was noted as a group that, along with their spin-off The Communards, continued to stand their ground and maintain a presence with their electronic sound. "Bronski beat and their spin off the Comming Arts stood their ground."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Post-Smiths Career as Session Guitarist
xref.body: After The Smiths' breakup, Johnny Marr became a highly sought-after session guitarist. He worked and toured with The Pretenders and Dada, and later co-founded Electronic with Barney Sumner of New Order. He also became a friend and confidante of Noel Gallagher of Oasis, collaborating with him in the studio, and worked with artists like Beth Orton, Neil Finn, Paul McCartney, and Talking Heads. "Meanwhile, Johnny Mar became a very hot session guitarist, working in touring with the pretenders in Dada."

xref.title: Preserving Guitar Music
xref.body: Death Leopard was a band that "made sure that guitars didn't disappear entirely" during eras like Synth Pop and Acid House when electronic music was prominent.

xref.body: The Human League served as Trent Reznor's "true inspiration" for becoming a musician. Their use of synthesizers and drum machines profoundly influenced him, more so than the punk bands of the era, shaping his early appreciation for electronic music. xref.title: Profound Influence
xref.body: David Bowie is considered one of the most influential musicians ever, arguably influencing more musical genres than even The Beatles due to his constant reinvention. His artistic DNA can be found across glam, punk, art rock, folk, hard rock, grunge, industrial music, electronic music, indie rock, and hip-hop. He brought an unprecedented level of sophistication to rock music, and his work continues to be studied, finding new fans across generations. "His DNA can be found in glam, punk, art rock folk, hard rock, grunge, industrial music, electronic music of all flavors, indie rock, and hip-hop."

xref.body: Spent much of the 1990s working as a programmer for various electronic artists. "He spent much of the 90s as a programmer for a variety of electronic artists."

xref.title: Prominent Technopop Band
xref.body: Men Without Hats was included in the roster of bands that reached commercial success during the peak of Technopop in the early 1980s, known for their accessible and danceable electronic music. "They were joined by bands like Durant, Rand, Soft Cell, OMD, ABC, DePesh Mode, Oflaca Seagulls, Men Without Hats, and so many others."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Prophetic Musical Vision
xref.body: Bowie possessed an unparalleled ability to "see 'round corners and predicted the future of rock," evolving through genres from folk to glam, blue-eyed soul, electronic, early industrial, and Technopop, demonstrating an extraordinary foresight in music trends. "Bowie saw round corners and predicted the future of rock unlike anyone we've ever seen."

xref.title: Punk Sensibility of Electronic Music (1970s-1980s)
xref.body: The band viewed their use of synths, playing with just two fingers, as an electronic equivalent to the punk rock aesthetic of thrashing a single guitar chord. They embraced electronics to create novel sounds, rejecting what they saw as "rock and roll cliches" of guitar, bass, and drums. "It was the punk sensibility, you know, just, instead of just thrashing one chord on a guitar, we were just playing with two fingers on synths and it was the same thing."

xref.body: Adrian Sherwood created "pretty radical remixes" for Depeche Mode songs like "People Are People" and "Master and Servant," characterized by heavy percussion, electronic rhythm, distortion, and tape loops. These remixes were highly influential, particularly on Al Jourgensen of Ministry. "Adrian had created some pretty radical remixes for Depeche Mode, most notably for people are people and master and servant."

xref.body: After failed attempts to create an electronic-tinged record with producers like The Chemical Brothers or David Bowie, the band decided to revert to the "punk funk" style that made "Blood Sugar Sex Magik" successful, an approach that proved fruitful for "Californication." xref.body: Some of David Bowie's electronic experiments exhibited a similar robotic, cold, artificial, emotionally sterile, and intense vibe to early Technopop artists like Kraftwerk and The Normal. xref.title: Robovox Creation
xref.body: Florian Schneider, a founding member of Kraftwerk, personally built an instrument called the Robovox. This custom-made device was used to treat vocals in a distinctive electronic way, contributing to the band's innovative sound, particularly on their 1974 "Autobahn" album. "something called a Robovox, which Florian Schneider built himself so he could treat vocals in a cool electronic way."

xref.body: An electronic album released in 1968 by Les Baxter was sampled in the Beastie Boys' song "Intergalactic," specifically appearing just after the one-minute mark. "This electronic album from 1968 is by Les Baxter, and it's in the song starting just after the one-minute mark."

xref.body: Morris built a sequencer that was crucial for connecting to New Order's Emulator sampler and orchestrating the various electronic elements of "Blue Monday." "He built a sequencer that could be connected to the band's new sampler, a keyboard called an emulator."

xref.title: Sequencing Bass Line Idea
xref.body: Bernard Sumner, the singer for New Order, originated the idea of sequencing a bass line from Peter Hook. This concept was pivotal in establishing the foundations of a new song played entirely by machines, influencing the band's future electronic direction. "It was singer Bernard Sumner who came up with the idea of sequencing a line in from bass player Peter Hook."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Serious Electronic Music
xref.body: For Kraftwerk, electronic music was a profound artistic pursuit, not a fleeting trend. It necessitated rigorous study, advanced engineering, and the construction of new musical instruments, underscoring their commitment to evolving the genre. "The electronic music was serious business. It required study and engineering and the building of new machines."

xref.title: Sex Change and New Identity
xref.body: After achieving success with pioneering electronic music and film scores, Walter Carlos underwent a sex change operation, funded by the profits from these ventures. Wendy Carlos now lives and works in New York City. "The profits from those bold synthesizer experiments paid for a sex change operation, and now Wendy Carlos lives and works in New York City."

xref.title: Sustained Success with Modified Sound
xref.body: Even as the popularity of pure Technopop declined through the mid-1980s, Depeche Mode managed to maintain its presence in the music scene. They continued to evolve their sound, adapting and modifying their electronic style to remain relevant beyond the genre's peak. "Depeche Mode stuck around, but with a modified sound."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Synth Experimentation and Production
xref.body: Giorgio Moroder, an Italian musician, was a pioneer in experimenting with new synthesizers as they emerged. His work, particularly his production of Donna Summer's "I Feel Love" in 1977, was highly influential, shaping the sound of disco with robotic, futuristic elements and inspiring countless electronic and technopop bands. Moroder's innovations drew a direct line to groups like Depeche Mode, OMD, and the Human League, and even inspired David Bowie, serving as a gateway to electronic music and Kraftwerk for many fans. "He had an extraordinarily big hit in 1977 with this song."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Synthesizer Automation
xref.body: Gillian Gilbert's synthesizers became an integral part of New Order's evolving electronic setup. A sequencer was used to automate keyboard parts and trigger sounds on her synthesizers, contributing to the band's distinctive new sound. "had it trigger something on Jillian Gilbert synthesizers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Synthesizer Discovery and Creative Shift
xref.body: In the spring of 1979, Gary Numan, who had previously favored guitars, encountered a Mini-Moog synthesizer in a studio. This spontaneous discovery radically altered his musical direction, leading him to abandon plans for a punk album and instead explore the concept of electronic punk songs, marking a pivotal moment in his career and the development of Technopop. "Another milestone in the creation of Tectopop came in the spring of 1979, when Gary Newman, previously a big fan of guitars, started playing with the new synthesizer someone had left in a studio, was a mini-mog."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Toronto-Based Indie/Industrial/Electronic Group
xref.body: Jackalope was an indie, industrial, and electronic music group based in Toronto. "They were an indie slash industrial slash electronic group from Toronto."

xref.title: Trent Reznor's View
xref.body: Trent Reznor acknowledged punk bands like the Sex Pistols as "cool," but found the electronic sounds of synthesizers and drum machines from bands like The Human League to be "really cool," indicating a preference for synth-driven music. "Punk bands like the Sex Bistles and the Clash and the Remones were cool and everything. But the synthesizers and drum machines of the human league and OMD and Depeche mode. Now that was really cool."

xref.title: Upbeat Electronic Pop
xref.body: Their first single, released in May 1979, showcased a unique style of electronic pop music that, unlike Kraftwerk's sound, was upbeat, happy, and described as "holds full." "Not only was their music completely electronic, but unlike craftwork, OMD's band of pop music was upbeat, happy, and there we say it. Holds full."

xref.title: Use of Flesh-and-Blood Drummer
xref.body: Unlike some contemporary electronic bands, Numan notably insisted on retaining a human drummer. "unlike Gary Newman who insisted on keeping a flesh and blood drummer, this group used recorded beats played off a real-to-real tape machine on stage."

xref.title: Visual Style Influence
xref.body: Kraftwerk's distinctive electronic sound inspired a corresponding visual aesthetic. Unlike the disheveled appearance of punks, their look featured sharp suits, ties, and meticulously groomed hair, projecting a cold and detached image. "This sound spawned a look. No scruffy punks here. Like war, sharpsuits and ties and had perfectly groomed hair."

xref.title: Volkswagen Beetle Samples
xref.body: Some of the unique sounds on Kraftwerk's track "Autobahn" were sourced from Ralf Hütter's Volkswagen Beetle. These sounds were captured by a tape recorder hanging out the window during a drive down the A555 autobahn, which links Bonn and Cologne, a major center for electronic music experimentation at the time. "Some of the sounds on this track are taken from Ralph Hooder's Volkswagen Beetle, captured by a taper quarter hanging out the window on a way down their highway called the A555."

xref.body: Burial, an electronic musician from London, released music completely anonymously for many years. "For years this electronic musician from London released music completely anonymously."
